newsitem.title: CHINA: China defends selection of HK post-colonial chief.
newsitem.headline: China defends selection of HK post-colonial chief.

text.p: Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen on Saturday defended the selection process of the first post-colonial chief executive of Hong Kong, saying it is democratic and reflects the virtues of the Chinese people.
"The democracy that we want to set up in Hong Kong...is different from the mainland and different from the West," Qian told the Preparatory Committee in Beijing.
"The selection process of the first chief executive is a democratic and civilised process and should reflect the virtues of our nationality," Qian said.
Qian heads the Beijing-selected committee, which is charged with transforming the British colony of Hong Kong into a Special Administrative Region of China after midnight on June 30, 1997.

The committee will meet again in Beijing November 1-2 to choose the 400 members of the Selection Committee, Chen Ziying, deputy director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office under the cabinet, told a news conference.
The Selection Committee will in turn elect the first person to lead Hong Kong after the wealthy but nervous territory of six million people reverts to Chinese rule.
In September, nearly 6,000 Hong Kong residents applied for a place on the Selection Committee.
Chen, the deputy director, said he expected Hong Kong's first post-colonial chief executive to be selected before Christmas.
Candidates to succeed Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten include two shipping tycoons, two former judges and a top woman civil servant.
Minister Qian told Preparatory Committee members not to believe rumours that members of the Selection Committee will be chosen by the emperor -- meaning the central government in Beijing.
During a two-day session which ended on Saturday, the Preparatory Committee passed draft regulations governing the selection of Hong Kong's post-colonial chief executive and an interim legislature.
The 60-member interim legislature will be in place for one year -- the terms of members will end on June 30, 1998, Chen said.

China has decided to dissolve Hong Kong's current Legislative Council and replace it with the interim parliament after Patten revised election rules in a move that Beijing says violated terms of the handover of the British colony.
Minister Qian defended the controversial interim legislature, saying the views of Hong Kong residents were fully solicited on the issue.
